summary: Describes a minimal framework for a new device, the pledge, to securely join a 6TiSCH network. The pledge and the central Join Registrar/Coordinator share a symmetric key, whose provisioning is out of scope.

eli5.summary: A new sensor uses a pre-shared secret to prove it is allowed to join the network, like a password for a club.

questions: how do devices join a 6tisch network
what is the constrained join protocol
how does a device join a 6tisch network
subtitle: How a brand-new low-power wireless device proves itself and gets its network keys in one secured request and response.

tldr.problem: A new device (a pledge) that wants to join a 6TiSCH low-power wireless network has no link-layer keys yet, so it cannot talk securely, and the network must not be easy to flood with bogus join traffic.
tldr.mechanism: The pledge and a central Join Registrar/Coordinator (JRC) share a unique symmetric key. The pledge sends one CoAP request protected by OSCORE through a Join Proxy, and the JRC answers with link-layer keys, a short address and other parameters.
tldr.outcome: The JRC can later push updates, such as new keys, over the same secure channel. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated.

today: RFC 9031 is a Proposed Standard published in May 2021, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on the 6TiSCH architecture in RFC 9030.

sections.title: The Secure Join Problem
sections.content:
RFC 9031 defines the Constrained Join Protocol (CoJP), a minimal "secure join" solution for a new device, called a pledge, to join a 6TiSCH network (IPv6 over the Time-Slotted Channel Hopping mode of IEEE 802.15.4). Secure join means network access authentication, authorization and parameter distribution, as framed in RFC 9030.

6TiSCH nodes keep their radios off most of the time to save energy, so the joining link has little bandwidth, and their microcontrollers have little code memory. The design therefore keeps over-the-air exchanges to a minimum and reuses protocols already in the stack: CoAP (RFC 7252) and OSCORE (RFC 8613).

CoJP assumes a central Join Registrar/Coordinator (JRC). The pledge and the JRC share a unique symmetric pre-shared key (PSK). How the PSK gets installed is out of scope.
sections.eli5: A tiny battery-powered gadget wants to join a network without wasting energy. It uses a secret it already shares with the network's boss so it can join with just one message back and forth.

sections.title: Provisioning and the Join Process
sections.content:
Before joining, the pledge is provisioned with a pledge identifier, which MUST be unique among all identifiers managed by a JRC (typically the 64-bit EUI-64 of the device), and a PSK. Each pledge MUST have a unique PSK with at least 128 bits of entropy, and the PSK MUST be changed when a device is recommissioned to a new owner. A network identifier (usually the 16-bit PAN ID) is optional but RECOMMENDED; without it the pledge must try one advertised network at a time, which prolongs joining.

The join then has three steps:

  • The pledge listens for an Enhanced Beacon (EB) from a node already in the network. That node acts as the Join Proxy (JP).
  • The pledge forms its link-local IPv6 address and may do Neighbor Discovery with the JP.
  • The pledge sends a Join Request via the JP to the JRC and receives a Join Response.

The pledge only talks to the JP, so it does not need to know how far away the JRC is. A 6LBR pledge (a border router joining over another network interface) skips the JP and talks to the JRC directly.
sections.eli5: The new gadget waits until it hears a neighbor shouting that the network exists. Then it asks that neighbor to pass its note to the boss and carry the answer back.

sections.title: Link, Network and Application Layer Setup
sections.content:
At the link layer, any node sending EBs MUST be prepared to act as a JP. The pledge has no link-layer keys, so it sends unsecured frames, and the JP must accept them for the duration of the join, for example by setting the secExempt attribute. To protect the pledge's sense of time against replayed beacons, all frames the JP sends to the pledge during the join MUST be authenticated at the link layer with the network's normal key. The pledge's own link-layer check will fail at first, and once the Join Response is processed successfully the pledge's Absolute Slot Number is declared valid.

At the network layer, the pledge and JP SHOULD keep a separate neighbor cache for untrusted entries. The JP SHOULD mark forwarded join traffic with the AF43 DSCP, and the JRC SHOULD mark Join Responses with AF42. Scheduling functions SHOULD NOT allocate extra cells for AF43 traffic. The JP caps outgoing join traffic, following the recommendation of 1 packet per 3 seconds from RFC 8085.

At the application layer the pledge is a CoAP client, the JRC is a CoAP server, and the JP is a CoAP forward proxy without a cache. The JP is RECOMMENDED to be stateless: it stores per-pledge state in the CoAP token (using extended tokens from RFC 8974) and forwards requests as non-confirmable messages, so the pledge does the retransmitting.
sections.eli5: The neighbor helping the newcomer is careful: it does not keep a diary of strangers, it limits how much mail it passes along, and it labels that mail so the rest of the network does not waste effort on it.

sections.title: Securing the Channel with OSCORE
sections.content:
The OSCORE security context is derived from the provisioned parameters: the Master Secret MUST be the PSK, the Master Salt MUST be the empty byte string, the ID Context MUST be the pledge identifier, the pledge's own ID is the empty byte string, and the JRC's ID is 0x4a5243 ("JRC" in ASCII). The default AEAD algorithm is AES-CCM-16-64-128, which gives an 8-byte authentication tag and 13-byte nonces, and the default key derivation function is HKDF with SHA-256.

The same context is reused later when the JRC acts as a client and the joined node as a server. Both sides MUST implement replay protection, and mutable context state (sender sequence number, replay window) MUST be kept in persistent memory so that nonces are never reused after reboots. OSCORE errors during joining MUST be silently dropped, and the pledge MUST silently discard any response not protected with OSCORE. This stops an attacker from forging error responses that would push the pledge to try one network after another.
sections.eli5: The secret password is used to scramble every message, and both sides keep careful count so an old message cannot be replayed. If something looks wrong, they stay quiet instead of answering, so trouble-makers learn nothing.

sections.title: CoJP Messages and Objects
sections.content:
CoJP payloads are encoded in CBOR. The Join Request is a CoAP POST, Confirmable, with Proxy-Scheme coap, Uri-Host 6tisch.arpa and Uri-Path j. Its payload is a Join_Request map holding the requested role (0 for a regular 6TiSCH node, 1 for a 6LBR), the network identifier (always included) and optionally an Unsupported Configuration object. The Join Response is a CoAP 2.04 (Changed) response carrying a Configuration object.

The Configuration object can hold: a link-layer key set, a short identifier, the JRC's IPv6 address (16 bytes), a blacklist of pledge identifiers the JP must silently drop, and a join rate that sets the JP's CoAP PROBING_RATE (zero means drop all join traffic).

Each link-layer key carries a key_id, an optional key_usage (default 0, 6TiSCH-K1K2-ENC-MIC32), the key_value and optional key_addinfo. The maximum key_id for IEEE 802.15.4 key index modes is 254. Implementations MUST use different keys for different MIC lengths. A short identifier must be 2 bytes long for IEEE 802.15.4, the values 0xfffe and 0xffff are invalid, and it must never be assigned twice under the same link-layer key because the short address feeds the link-layer nonce.
sections.eli5: The request is a short form saying who is asking and which network. The answer is a packet with the network's keys, a short nickname for the newcomer, and some rules about how much it may help others.

sections.title: Updates, Rekeying and Failures
sections.content:
After joining, the node becomes a CoAP server exposing the /j resource at Uri-Host 6tisch.arpa. The JRC sends a Parameter Update (a Confirmable POST with a Configuration object) to change settings such as keys. CoAP Observe is not feasible here because the node's IPv6 address changes when it gets a global address.

For rekeying, a 6LBR MUST immediately start using new keys for outgoing traffic and drop old keys after COJP_REKEYING_GUARD_TIME (recommended 12 seconds). A regular node installs the new keys, accepts both old and new for incoming traffic, keeps using the old keys until it receives traffic secured with the new ones, and then switches, creating a ripple of updates.

If a pledge cannot act on a Join Response parameter, it SHOULD retry and include an Unsupported Configuration object, up to COJP_MAX_JOIN_ATTEMPTS (recommended 4). A request with unsupported parameters gets a Diagnostic Response with code 4.00 (Bad Request). If the JRC loses its security context state, it can answer the first Join Request with 4.01 (Unauthorized) and a nonce of at least 8 bytes, following Appendix B.2 of RFC 8613, so a fresh context can be negotiated.
sections.eli5: Later, the boss can send new keys to everyone. Nodes switch over one neighbor at a time, like a rumor spreading, and keep the old key briefly so nobody gets locked out.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Notes
sections.content:
The pledge identifier is sent in the clear as the OSCORE kid context, so using a globally unique EUI-64 has privacy risks discussed in RFC 7721, such as correlating activity over time and location tracking. As a mitigation, the JRC may assign a short address that SHOULD be uncorrelated with the long-term identifier; an eavesdropper may still correlate them by timing, less so when many pledges join at once.

On the security side, the RFC warns that a single PSK shared across a group of devices is a common pitfall, as is deriving "unique" PSKs by hashing serial numbers or EUI-64s. It recommends cryptographically secure random generation. A pledge cannot verify EBs when it first synchronizes, so attackers can craft fake beacons; the pledge can keep a temporary blacklist of bad EBs, limited by its memory. The shared minimal cell used for join traffic can be congested by an attacker, which redundant JPs help alleviate.
sections.eli5: Shouting your unique serial number can let snoopers follow you around, so the boss can hand out a nickname instead. And never reuse one secret across many gadgets, or one stolen gadget spills the secret for all of them.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: The RFC requests the well-known name 6tisch.arpa under the .arpa name space, with no subdomains expected and no A, AAAA or PTR records requested. It also creates three subregistries in the "IPv6 Over the TSCH Mode of IEEE 802.15.4 (6TiSCH)" registry: CoJP Parameters, CoJP Key Usage and CoJP Unsupported Configuration Codes. Integer values from -256 to 255 are Standards Action, values from 256 to 65535 and from -65536 to -257 are Specification Required, values above 65535 are Expert Review, and values below -65536 are Private Use.
sections.eli5: The authors asked for an official name for the boss and set up public lists of the codes used in the messages, so everyone uses the same numbers.
